newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt markets close weaker after wages data.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt markets close weaker after wages data.

* NZ debt markets weaken after wages data
* Mixed views on what "neutral" data means for Reserve Bank
* Bonds sell off, seen weaker as Greenspan testimony looms
New Zealand debt markets closed weaker on Tuesday after November quarter wages data, while largely in line with expectations, confirmed that the economy continues to grow, dealers said.
The Quarterly Employment Survey released by Statistics New Zealand showed total average hourly ordinary time earnings rose 0.7 percent in the November quarter and 3.5 percent in the November year.

"They were pretty well on expectations, I think, for most parties, but at the end of the day it was just a continuation of the numbers that we've had over the last couple of weeks that suggest the economy is growing pretty well and pretty strongly," said a dealer.

The 90-day bank bill rate spiked about five points higher after the release, although dealers said the short end remained within its present range and looked unlikely to break out of it in the medium term.
The consensus among market watchers was that the data were neutral for the Reserve Bank, which will release its six-monthly economic projections on March 13.
Some bank economists said the wages numbers did nothing to alter their view that there was room for the central bank to ease monetary conditions slightly in the first half of 1997.
"They must be long," the dealer said.
"Until the whole property picture, especially in Auckland, starts to calm down, I really don't think they (the RBNZ) can justify any easing."
In the bond market, rates also spiked higher, but dealers said the wages data had only contributed to an already bearish tone.

"The market is being sold off quite aggressively in the long end, basically on what's happening in Australia -- they're off eight basis points in their ten-years, and we're off about the same," said one senior dealer.
He said the bond market's focus had now turned towards Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony before the Senate mid-week.
The market would be nervous about Greenspan's testimony, given some of his recent comments, the dealer said.
"I think we'll see a gradual rise in rates from where we are. I think everything has been pushing towards a more bearish market."
